text.p: These are the leading stories in the Sarajevo press on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Bosnian companies which own holiday resorts along the Adriatic coast in Croatia cannot use them until the problem of the ownership of Bosnian companies in Croatia and Croatian companies in Bosnia is resolved, Croatian tourism company official Mili Razovic says in an interview.

- NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) stepped up its patrols on the former frontline between the Croat and Moslem-held parts of Mostar in order to secure freedom of movement and safety of all the citizens.

- Moslem co-prime minister in Bosnian government, Haris Silajdzic, meets the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) chairman Niels Halvag Petersen in Sarajevo and says his government is not completely satisfied with the OSCE's work in Bosnia.

- Head of Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation's police department says that preparations for Pope John Paul's visit to Sarajevo, scheduled for April 12-13, are carried out in a complex situation in the federation, but the police is capable of providing security for all participants in the event.
- Bosnian Serb officials held talks with the World Bank's officials and agreed that assistance to Bosnian entities hinges on a deal with the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

- Prime minister of Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation government, Edhem Bicakcic, says he requested greater contributions from the United States in deblocking the work of federal institutions and the establishment of the central bank.

- The World Bank is currently working on implementation of 16 Bosnia projects worth a total of $360 million, $210 million of which had allready been spent on the ground, the bank executive director for Central and Eastern Europe, Christine Wallich, says.

- If things continue to move this way there is a chance that Dayton peace accord could be changed and we are doing our best to prevent that, Moslem co-prime minister in Bosnian government, Haris Silajdzic, says.

- Officials from the U.S. embassy in Sarajevo and the office of the International High Representative for Bosnia, Carl Bildt, think that the Dayton peace accord must not be changed but implemented thouroughly.

- The last mosque placed at the left bank of the Neretva river in the Croat held Bosnian town of Capljina has been damaged in an explosion set by Bosnian Croat extremists on March 10, town's officials in exile say.
- 19 suicides were registred in February on the territory of Moslem-Croat federation, federal interior ministry says.

- U.S. oil company Amoco announces it will come to Bosnia to check if it is rich with oil, prime minister of Bosnia's Moslem- Croat federal government Edhem Bicakcic says after visiting the United States.
- International supervision over the disputed Bosnian town of Brcko will begin on April 1, instead of March 22, the town's official Munib Jusufovic says.
- Croatian president Franjo Tudjman and country's defence minister Gojko Susak are not tearing Bosnia apart, Croatian ambassador to Bosnia, Darinko Bago says.
